nodes.title: Kubernetes Deployment strategies: Key Ideas
nodes.content: A Kubernetes Deployment manages rolling updates and rollbacks for stateless Pods. CKAD exams test strategy types, rollout commands, and how resource limits interact with scheduling.

flashcards.back: RollingUpdate: gradually replaces old Pods with new ones (zero downtime). Recreate: terminates all old Pods before starting new ones (brief downtime).

flashcards.front: maxSurge and maxUnavailable — what do they control?
flashcards.back: maxSurge: how many extra Pods above the desired count can exist during rollout. maxUnavailable: how many Pods can be down at once. Both accept absolute numbers or percentages.

flashcards.front: Command to roll back a Deployment to the previous revision?
flashcards.back: kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>  (add --to-revision=N to target a specific revision from rollout history).
Liveness: kills and restarts the container if it fails. Readiness: removes the Pod from Service endpoints if it fails (does not restart).

questions.q: You are bootstrapping an Azure Machine Learning workspace. Which set of associated Azure resources is provisioned automatically when you create a workspace through the Azure portal default flow?
choices: Storage account, Key Vault, Application Insights, and Container Registry
SQL Database, Cosmos DB, Event Hub, and Log Analytics workspace
Synapse workspace, Data Lake Storage Gen2, Purview, and Container Registry
Storage account, Service Bus namespace, Front Door, and Azure Monitor workspace
questions.explanation: An Azure ML workspace requires four linked resources: a Storage account (default datastore for data and run artefacts), a Key Vault (secrets, connection strings), Application Insights (metrics and telemetry), and an Azure Container Registry (training and inference images). ACR is created lazily on first use unless you pre-attach one. Synapse, SQL, Cosmos DB, Event Hub and Service Bus are not part of the workspace's default footprint.

questions.q: A data scientist needs an always-available, single-user development environment in Azure ML for interactive notebook work and lightweight model prototyping, with no requirement to scale across nodes. Which compute target is the best fit?
choices: Compute cluster (autoscaling multi-node training)
Inference cluster on Azure Kubernetes Service
Compute instance (managed single-user VM)
Attached Azure Databricks compute
questions.explanation: A compute instance is a managed single-user VM intended for development: it ships with notebooks, the v2 SDK and CLI, and common ML libraries preinstalled, and supports schedule-based auto-start/stop to control cost. Compute clusters autoscale across nodes for training and batch scoring; AKS inference clusters host real-time endpoints; attached Databricks is for Spark workloads — none of these are the right shape for individual interactive notebooks.

questions.q: You want to define a reusable, schema-rich data asset that points at multiple Parquet files in Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 and lets training scripts read it as a pandas or Spark DataFrame with consistent column types. Which data asset type should you create in Azure ML v2?
choices: uri_file (single immutable file pointer)
mltable (tabular schema with transformations)
uri_folder (folder path reference)
Datastore credential (storage account binding)
questions.explanation: An mltable data asset wraps a YAML definition (MLTable file) that specifies the source paths, file format, column types and lightweight transformations such as take, filter or convert_column_types. Training code calls mltable.load() and gets a typed DataFrame back. uri_file and uri_folder return raw paths without schema, and a datastore is a credential mapping to a storage container, not a data asset.

questions.q: You submit an Automated ML classification job in Azure ML and want to ensure the run optimises for recall on the positive class while still avoiding training-time data leakage. Which configuration is correct?
choices: Set primary_metric=accuracy and disable featurization
Set primary_metric=AUC_weighted and skip the validation split
Set primary_metric=spearman_correlation and use a leave-one-out split
Set primary_metric=norm_macro_recall and enable featurization with auto cross-validation
questions.explanation: norm_macro_recall is the AutoML classification metric that captures balanced recall across classes and is the closest of the built-in choices to optimising for true-positive rate. Automatic featurization plus AutoML's k-fold cross-validation (or a held-out validation set) prevents leakage from preprocessing learned on the entire dataset. Accuracy hides class imbalance, AUC_weighted measures ranking quality (not recall directly), and spearman_correlation is a regression-only metric.

questions.q: Which import path corresponds to the supported Azure ML Python SDK v2 client used in DP-100 study materials?
choices: from azure.ai.ml import MLClient
from azureml.core import Workspace
from azureml.train.estimator import Estimator
from azure.mgmt.machinelearningservices import MachineLearningServicesMgmtClient
questions.explanation: The SDK v2 client lives in the azure.ai.ml package, and MLClient is its entry point for managing assets, jobs, components and endpoints. azureml.core.Workspace and azureml.train.estimator.Estimator are SDK v1 surfaces (still readable but no longer the recommended path), and azure.mgmt.machinelearningservices is the ARM/management SDK used for provisioning workspaces, not for training jobs.

questions.q: You want to run a hyperparameter search across a large continuous learning-rate range while terminating clearly underperforming trials early to save compute. Which combination should you configure in an Azure ML sweep job?
choices: Grid sampling with no early-termination policy
Bayesian sampling with the median-stopping policy
Bayesian sampling with the truncation-selection policy
Random sampling with the Bandit early-termination policy
questions.explanation: Random sampling is the most flexible choice for continuous ranges and integrates with every early-termination policy; the Bandit policy stops trials whose primary metric falls outside a configurable slack of the current best run, which is the most aggressive way to reclaim compute. Grid sampling does not support continuous spaces well and the question specifies early termination is wanted. Bayesian sampling in Azure ML does NOT support early-termination policies, so the two Bayesian options are invalid.

questions.q: Inside a training script running on Azure ML you want to log parameters, metrics and the trained scikit-learn model to the workspace so it appears under the job's Outputs + logs and in the model registry. Which approach matches the v2 guidance?
choices: Print metrics to stdout and rely on the run's captured log file
Call Run.get_context().log() and Model.register() from azureml.core
Use the MLflow tracking and models APIs (mlflow.log_metric, mlflow.sklearn.log_model)
Write a metrics.json file to ./outputs and download it after the run
questions.explanation: Azure ML uses MLflow as the native tracking and model-packaging layer in SDK v2: mlflow.log_param, mlflow.log_metric and mlflow.<flavor>.log_model write straight into the workspace, and the tracking URI is configured automatically inside an Azure ML job. Run.get_context().log() and Model.register() are the SDK v1 surface. Printing to stdout does not produce metric charts, and writing files to ./outputs persists artefacts but does not register a model.

questions.q: Your team needs low-latency real-time scoring with traffic splitting between a current model and a new candidate, ideally on managed Microsoft infrastructure so the team does not own a Kubernetes cluster. Which Azure ML deployment target should you choose?
choices: Managed online endpoint with two deployments and weighted traffic
Batch endpoint with parallel deployment job
Kubernetes online endpoint on a self-managed AKS cluster
Local Docker deployment exposed through Azure Front Door
questions.explanation: Managed online endpoints are Microsoft-hosted compute that expose a stable scoring URL and host one or more deployments behind it; you assign weighted traffic (e.g., 90/10) for blue-green or canary rollouts. Batch endpoints are for asynchronous scoring of large datasets, not low-latency requests. Kubernetes online endpoints work but require you to attach and operate the AKS cluster. Local Docker is for dev/testing only.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.

questions.q: A training workload runs a few times per week, needs 4 GPU nodes while running, and should cost nothing between runs. Which Azure ML compute target fits?
choices: A compute instance resized to a GPU SKU and left running so jobs can start instantly
An attached Azure Databricks cluster configured with GPU workers and auto-termination
A compute cluster with GPU SKU, min nodes 0 and max nodes 4
An Azure Kubernetes Service inference cluster with GPU node pools enabled
questions.explanation: Compute clusters autoscale between their min and max node counts; with min=0 they deprovision entirely between jobs, so idle cost is zero. A compute instance is a single-user, always-on dev box; AKS targets are for inference; Databricks attachment is for Spark workloads and adds platform overhead this scenario doesn't need.

questions.q: During a hyperparameter sweep you want Azure ML to stop runs whose primary metric is clearly worse than the best runs so far, saving compute. What do you configure on the sweep job?
choices: An early termination policy such as bandit or median stopping
A lower max_total_trials value so the sweep submits fewer runs overall
A smaller search space so only promising configurations are sampled
A timeout on the parent pipeline so the sweep cannot exceed its budget
questions.explanation: Early termination policies (bandit, median stopping, truncation selection) evaluate each trial's reported metric at intervals and cancel trials underperforming the current leaders — exactly the 'stop clearly worse runs' behavior. Fewer trials, smaller spaces and timeouts all reduce total work but indiscriminately: they don't selectively kill bad runs while letting good ones finish.

questions.q: Training has produced a model file the team wants to version, share across the workspace, and reference by name when creating endpoints. What is the FIRST step?
choices: Upload the file to the workspace's default blob container under a folder named for the model
Register the model in the workspace model registry, creating a named, versioned asset
Create a managed online endpoint and embed the model file inside its scoring image
Commit the model binary to the team's Git repository alongside the training code
questions.explanation: Registering creates a first-class model asset — named, versioned, with lineage to the producing job — that deployments, pipelines and teammates reference by name:version. Raw blob uploads have no versioning semantics; endpoints consume registered models rather than embedding loose files; Git is for code, and large binaries don't belong in it.

questions.q: In Azure ML, what is the difference between a datastore and a data asset?
choices: A datastore caches data locally on the compute node, while a data asset always streams records directly from the source service
A datastore is created per job and deleted afterwards, while data assets persist across jobs
Datastores hold tabular data only, while data assets are required for files and folders
A datastore stores the connection to a storage service; a data asset is a versioned reference to specific data within it
questions.explanation: A datastore wraps the connection and credentials for a storage service (blob container, ADLS, file share); a data asset is a named, versioned pointer to particular files, folders or tables — typically resolved through a datastore. Neither dictates caching vs streaming by itself, datastores persist indefinitely, and both work with files and tabular data.

questions.q: A business analyst with no Python experience must assemble a training pipeline by connecting prebuilt data-prep and model components on a visual canvas. Which Azure ML feature do they use?
choices: The Designer
The VS Code extension with the Azure ML CLI v2 and YAML job definitions
Jupyter notebooks preinstalled on a workspace compute instance
The AutoML guided user interface in Azure ML studio
questions.explanation: The Designer is the drag-and-drop canvas: prebuilt and custom components are wired into pipelines without writing code. The CLI/YAML route and notebooks are code-first; AutoML automates model selection for a dataset but isn't a pipeline-composition canvas — you don't connect steps in it.

questions.q: Months after deployment, a model's accuracy is degrading. The team suspects the statistical distribution of incoming features has shifted from the training data. Which Azure ML capability detects this?
choices: Endpoint autoscaling rules comparing CPU and memory utilization against historical baselines
Data drift monitoring comparing production input distributions against a baseline dataset
Application Insights availability tests probing the endpoint on a fixed schedule
Re-running the original training job to verify the code still produces the same model
questions.explanation: Model monitoring/data drift detection profiles the features arriving at the endpoint and statistically compares them with the training (baseline) distribution, alerting when drift exceeds thresholds — the canonical signal that retraining is due. Autoscaling and availability tests watch infrastructure health, and re-training reproducibility says nothing about today's input data.

questions.q: You submit an AutoML classification job with training data but no validation dataset. How does AutoML obtain a validation estimate by default?
choices: It skips validation entirely and reports metrics computed on the training data itself
It requires you to attach a labeled test dataset before the job is allowed to start
It automatically applies cross-validation or a train/validation split depending on data size
It deploys each candidate model to a temporary staging endpoint and scores live traffic for an hour
questions.explanation: When no validation data is supplied, AutoML applies its own validation strategy — k-fold cross-validation for smaller datasets or an automatic train/validation split for larger ones — so reported metrics are out-of-sample. It never silently scores on training data, doesn't demand a test set up front, and certainly doesn't validate against live traffic.

questions.q: Stakeholders want one view that combines model performance broken down by demographic cohort, error analysis, and feature importance to support a fairness review. What does Azure ML provide for this?
choices: The Responsible AI dashboard generated for the registered model
The Samples gallery of notebook tutorials inside Azure ML studio
The compute monitoring tab showing GPU utilization across training runs
The dataset profile view summarizing column statistics in the data asset
questions.explanation: The Responsible AI dashboard aggregates error analysis, fairness/cohort metrics, model explanations (feature importances), and counterfactual/causal components into a single interactive view tied to a registered model. Dataset profiles describe inputs only; compute monitoring and the samples gallery have nothing to do with fairness review.
